summary: Defines a DHCP relay agent information suboption that lets a relay replace the Server Identifier value inserted by the server. The relay can then receive renewal requests directly and add its own information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Clients normally talk straight to the DHCP server when renewing. This lets the go-between answer instead, so it can keep adding its notes.

questions: what is the dhcp server identifier override suboption
why do dhcp renewals bypass the relay
what is dhcp relay agent suboption 11
subtitle: How a DHCP relay can make clients send their lease renewals through it instead of straight to the server.

tldr.problem: After a lease is granted, a client in RENEWING state sends its DHCPREQUEST straight to the server named in the Server Identifier option, so a relay agent may never see it and cannot add its Relay Agent Information option.
tldr.mechanism: A new relay agent suboption, Server Identifier Override (code 11, length 4), carries an address that the DHCP server must place in the Server Identifier option of its replies, so the client sends renewals to the relay.
tldr.outcome: The server gets the same relay information on renewals as it did on the first DHCPDISCOVER. The catch is that the server must support the suboption, and the relay becomes a point of failure for renewals.

today: RFC 5107 is a Proposed Standard from February 2008 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Renewal Problem
sections.content:
A DHCP relay agent sits between clients and a server on another network. It can easily insert a Relay Agent Information option, described in RFC 3046, with suboptions such as Circuit-ID, Remote-ID and Device Class into DHCPDISCOVER messages.

Once a lease has been granted, though, a client in RENEWING state sends its DHCPREQUEST directly to the server named in the Server Identifier option. Depending on the network topology, the relay may not see these RENEW DHCPREQUEST messages, so it cannot insert its information into them.

The new suboption lets the relay tell the server what value to put in the Server Identifier option. The relay can then force a renewing host to send DHCPREQUEST messages to the relay, which adds its information and relays the message to the real server. The server therefore sees the same relay information on renewals as on the first DHCPDISCOVER. The RFC notes that this lets the DHCPv4 relay work the way the DHCPv6 relay already does.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a receptionist who stamps every visitor's form with the visitor's room number. When you come back later you walk straight to the manager and skip the receptionist, so there is no stamp. This fix makes you go through the receptionist again.

sections.title: The Suboption Format
sections.content:
The Server Identifier Override suboption has a code of 11 and a length field n that is always 4. It is followed by four octets, a1 through a4, which hold the overriding server identifier address.

Those four octets are the value that the DHCP server MUST insert into the Server Identifier option when it replies.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny label with a type number, a length, and one address. The address says: when you write your name on the reply, write this name instead.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
A server that implements the suboption MUST use the value, if present in a message from a client, as the Server Identifier in its response. It must also record the address for use in later messages to that client, until the next DHCP message arrives from the relay agent.

Normally a server checks the Server Identifier in a DHCPREQUEST against its own interface addresses and silently ignores the request if it does not match. If the message carries the override suboption, the server instead compares the suboption's address with the Server Identifier option. If both give the same address, the server should accept the DHCPREQUEST for processing, whether or not that address matches one of its interfaces.

The relay agent still fills in the giaddr field when relaying, as it normally would.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server sees the go-between's name tag, it signs its replies with that name. Later, when a request comes back addressed to the go-between's name, the server knows that is fine and accepts it.

sections.title: Relay Behavior and Deployment Caveats
sections.content:
If the relay forwards to more than one server, it SHOULD forward all DHCP messages, including RENEW DHCPREQUESTs, to all of them. The intent is that the relay does not need to keep any state about the lease. Relays that implement this suboption SHOULD also implement and use the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Flags Suboption from RFC 5010, which tells the server whether the original message arrived as a broadcast or unicast.

A server that does not understand the suboption ignores it and inserts its own interface address, so the relay will not receive the renewals. An administrator configuring a relay to use the suboption should check that the target server supports it.

If the client cannot reach the relay, or the relay loses its connection to the server, later renewals may not be processed properly and the client's lease may time out.
sections.plainLanguage: The go-between should pass every message to every server so it does not have to remember anything. If the server does not know the trick, nothing changes. If the go-between goes offline, renewals get stuck and the client could lose its address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Relay Agent Information option relies on a trusted relationship between relay and server, as described in RFC 3046. A perimeter defense can block fraudulent relay options, but the RFC says a deeper defense using the authentication suboption of RFC 4030 SHOULD be deployed too.

A rogue relay placed between client and server could use this suboption to redirect clients to itself. It could then deny RENEW DHCPREQUESTs and force clients to stop using their addresses, or change, insert or delete options in DHCPACK messages and extend leases beyond what the server allowed. DHCP authentication (RFC 3118) and relay option authentication would address this.

The RFC says it adds no new vulnerabilities except where DHCP authentication is already in place and clients require it. The suboption is not meant to provide any security benefit by itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake go-between could pull clients toward itself and then cut them off or hand out wrong answers. Using signatures on the messages, so that fakes are caught, is the cure.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned suboption number 11 for the Server Identifier Override Suboption, taken from the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option suboption number space defined in RFC 3046.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of label numbers gave this new label the number 11, so everyone uses the same one.
